title: The census asks of faith and finds none to answer for some
summary: The state's first census, sent to ask what households hold to as well as how many they number, meets on the far north-western cape and its islets a good many who give no creed at all. Finding no word in Dia-thìris that fits a household with nothing to declare, the clerks write against their names gun chreideamh, without a creed, and ride on.

title: The two counts of Doire ghlas go uncorrected
summary: The state's roll and the Moot's own tally of the northern shire, taken the same season by different hands, are found afterward to differ by close to a fifth. Neither is sent to the other side to be checked against it, and both are filed, each true by its own reckoning, in the chest that kept it.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid's letter of office reaches Cathair dhomhain
summary: A council rider, delayed three days by flooded roads, brings Eilidh nic Leòid the letter naming her first among the circuit justices: eleven shires of the south-west to be ridden once in every twelvemonth, and a written record of every judgment to be carried back each year to the council's clerks.

title: Eilidh's first assize, held at Cathair dhomhain
summary: Before setting out on her circuit Eilidh nic Leòid sits her first cases at home: a boundary measured with a knotted cord rather than taken on either party's word, a debt found on the strength of an unburned receipt, and a fishmonger's short weight proved against the council's own standard.

title: The quarrel over the well at Muileann bhàn
summary: A widow who once charged a penny a season for water from a spring now run dry, and the mason set to warden the town's new waterworks, bring their dispute over one well to the circuit justice's bench in the mill-yard, the town having no courtroom of its own.

title: Eilidh's ruling on the Muileann bhàn well
summary: The justice rules that the dead spring's old custom cannot be transferred to water drawn by a different road and paid for from a different purse, but that the well's ground remains the widow's by custom, and the town's word is given that it will never be built over or fenced from her without leave.

title: The head-due first gathered along the southern circuit
summary: Maors' clerks set up their tables at the crossroads of the south-west shires and take the head-due, eighteen purses on every five thousand heads, for the first time in living memory. Eilidh nic Leòid, riding past more than one such table, keeps her own note of what she sees, though none of it is brought to her bench.

title: Eilidh's circuit calls at Inis thais
summary: The harbour court at Inis thais, kept well enough already by its own magistrate, hands up only two causes to the visiting justice, both turning on the ownership of a fishing boat after its owner died leaving no heir the town could agree on.

title: Eilidh's circuit calls at Doire shean
summary: Sitting two days in the temple porch for want of a courtroom, the justice settles a dispute among four households over the right to dry nets on a stretch of shingle by asking after the shore's own long custom rather than any written law, which none had ever thought to write so far down the coast.

title: The maor of Seann Bhral asks a ruling of his own cousin
summary: Artair mac Lachlainn, maor of the western shire, meets the circuit justice at the town gate and asks her plainly to find for the Crown's grant, the household holding it being kin of his own. She hears the cause as she hears any other, and he sits through it without speaking.

title: The Coyle suit heard at Seann Bhral in the west
summary: A Tuathaich family holding four fields under a Company surveyor's title cut before the Severance is set against a Dia-thìreach household holding the Crown's newer grant of the same ground, made in ignorance that the land was occupied at all. Half the shire's Tuathaich households come to Seann Bhral to hear it argued.

title: The Leòid ruling copied to every maor's court of the circuit
summary: Eilidh nic Leòid has her ruling fair-copied to every maor's court of her eleven shires, with a note that any like cause be decided on like reasoning until the council itself says otherwise, reasoning that a law read differently in every court that hears it is no law at all.
